hub_subtitle: From hesitant communicator to confident global business leader

lesson.menu_desc: Milton's business does not depend only on his clients: a strong dollar, a new tariff and a slowdown in the US can change a whole year. Before the biggest shipment of the year, he joins a briefing with Rebecca, an economist at his bank in Miami, and learns to explain the big picture in complex sentences that hold two ideas at once (although demand is strong, the new tariff will cut our margin; despite the slowdown, luxury is growing). Plus the language of international trade: tariff, exchange rate, inflation, recession, demand, commodity, customs, purchasing power — 35 slides

items.situation: Your US client asks why your prices went up. Give one reason in one sentence.
Sales are good, but your margin is smaller. Say both ideas in one sentence.
Tell your partner that luxury is still growing in a difficult economy.
Compare the US market with the Brazilian market.
Explain why the shipment is late.
Ask Rebecca what will happen to the dollar next year.

listenings.text: Good morning, and welcome to your Monday markets update. Let's start with the dollar. Although many experts expected it to fall this year, the dollar is still strong, and that is good news for exporters who sell in the United States. Next, inflation. Prices in the US rose two point nine percent last year, whereas in Europe the number was closer to two percent. Even though inflation is slowing, many families feel that their purchasing power is smaller than before. Now, gold. Because of the uncertainty in the world, investors are buying more of it, and the price of this commodity reached a new record last week. That is a problem for jewelers, because their raw material is more expensive. Finally, the big question: will there be a recession next year? Most economists say no. Despite the slowdown, demand for luxury goods is still growing, especially among the richest buyers. That's all for today. Have a good week, and see you next Monday.

My name is Ricardo, and I export leather bags from Brazil to the United States and Europe. People think exporting is about the product. It isn't. It's about the world. In 2015, Brazil was in a deep recession. Although my sales in Brazil fell by forty percent, my company survived, because of one decision I had made five years before. I had started selling abroad. Whereas my local clients stopped buying, my American clients kept ordering. And because the real was weak, my products were suddenly cheaper in dollars. The exchange rate saved my business. But the world can also hurt you. Two years ago, a new tariff on leather goods made my prices ten percent higher overnight. Even though my clients liked my bags, some of them changed to cheaper brands. My advice to any exporter is simple. Read the economic news every morning, the same way you read your sales numbers. You cannot control the dollar, a tariff or a recession. But you can be ready for them.
